summary: This standards-track document specifies an alternative way to validate certificates in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure, replacing the procedure from RFC 6487. It aims to reduce operational fragility in certificate management while keeping the essential security properties. It is meant to make the RPKI easier to run without breaking things.

eli5.summary: If a ticket has a small mistake, the whole line stops. This changes the ticket-checking rules to be less picky about harmless problems and still catch the real fakes.

questions: how to make rpki certificate validation less fragile
what is a verified resource set
what happens when an rpki certificate overclaims
do the new rpki oids change roa validation
subtitle: A gentler way to validate RPKI certificates: when a certificate claims too much, keep what is valid instead of rejecting it all.

tldr.problem: Under the RFC 6487 procedure, a Resource Certificate that overclaims any resources its issuer does not hold is rejected entirely, which also invalidates everything below it. Transfers, reclaimed resources or operational errors can cause this, even for objects that never use the overclaimed resources.
tldr.mechanism: A new certificate policy OID and new extension OIDs signal an alternative validation. Each certificate gets a Verified Resource Set, the intersection of its claimed resources with the set from its issuer, and an overclaim only produces a warning.
tldr.outcome: ROAs and router certificates are still valid only if all their resources are in the Verified Resource Set, so nothing unheld is accepted. If the new OIDs are not used, the outcome is the same as RFC 6487.

today: RFC 8360 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an alternative to the validation in RFC 6487, and the text leaves deployment to separate discussion.

sections.title: Overview of the Change
sections.content:
This document specifies an alternative to the certificate validation procedure in RFC 6487. The older procedure requires that a Resource Certificate be rejected entirely if it overclaims, meaning it includes Internet Number Resources (INRs) not contained in the certificate of the CA that issued it. The procedure here accepts such a certificate for the intersection of its resources and the issuing certificate's resources.

When no overclaims occur, both procedures give the same outcome. The new one can never accept resources that are not validly held along the path of issuing certificates. The damage from a lost resource is limited to the attestations, such as Route Origin Authorizations (RFC 6482), that actually refer to it.

Validation here considers a single trust anchor only. Overclaims where several configured trust anchors claim overlapping resources are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Before, one wrong item on a form made the whole form get thrown out. Now only the wrong item is crossed out, and the rest still counts.

sections.title: The Problem: Overclaiming
sections.content:
In the RPKI, each certificate in a chain must have resources that are encompassed by those of its issuer. The first certificate is a trust anchor, whose resources are valid by definition.

Resource transfers change what is recorded. CAs may update their certificates in an order that makes some of them overclaim temporarily. A child CA may not ask for a shrunk certificate when a parent reclaims resources, and operational errors in RPKI databases can also leave a CA certificate that no longer covers its subordinates.

The RFC's example: a trust anchor holds 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 2001:db8::/32 and AS64496-AS64500. CA1 is reissued without 198.51.100.0/24 but never reissues CA2's certificate. That certificate now overclaims and is invalid, and so is a ROA below it for 192.0.2.0/24 with ASN 64496, even though that ROA uses none of the removed space. CA1 could fix it by reissuing, but until then the ROA stays invalid.

The RFC calls this a low-probability problem today, but the impact on routing security would be high if it happened near the top of the hierarchy, since the whole subtree would be invalidated.
sections.eli5: A teacher takes one sticker off a page, and now a student's whole sticker book is declared invalid, even the stickers that were fine. That is not fair when most of it is still good.

sections.title: Verified Resource Sets
sections.content:
The change works by tracking a Verified Resource Set (VRS) for each certificate, separate from the resources written in its extensions. The algorithm keeps two: VRS-IP for address space and VRS-AS for AS numbers. Both start from the trust anchor's extension values.

For each later certificate, if the extension is present the VRS is the intersection of the certificate's resources with the VRS computed for its issuer. If the extension is absent, the VRS is NULL.

If the VRS differs from what the certificate claims, the result depends on the policy. Under the new policy a warning listing the overclaiming resources SHOULD be issued. Under the RFC 6487 policy the certificate MUST be rejected. A CA certificate with no resources in common with the path is not rejected immediately because the condition may be transient, and this is safe because the VRS accurately reflects what is validly held.
sections.eli5: Each certificate keeps a short list of what it is really allowed to have, made by comparing its own list with its parent's list. Anything extra is just left off, not trusted.

sections.title: Signalling the Alternative with New OIDs
sections.content:
The choice is signalled by new object identifiers. A new certificate policy, id-cp-ipAddr-asNumber-v2 (OID arc cp(14) 3), is the same as the policy in RFC 6484 but drives the decision in Step 8 of the validation. New extensions id-pe-ipAddrBlocks-v2 (id-pe 28) and id-pe-autonomousSysIds-v2 (id-pe 29) take the place of the RFC 3779 extensions, with the same syntax, and may only be used together with the new policy.

The profile follows RFC 6487 with some changes. The policy extension MUST be critical and contain exactly one policy of the new type. Either the IP or AS resources extension, or both, MUST be present and critical. The SAFI value MUST NOT be used, and Routing Domain Identifier values MUST NOT be used. Each extension must be a non-empty set or use inherit.

The document also assigns new ASN.1 module OIDs, 90 and 91, including an addendum to RFC 6268. If the new OIDs are not used under a trust anchor, the outcome matches RFC 6487.
sections.eli5: Certificates carry a label saying which rulebook to use. A new label means 'use the forgiving rulebook', and the old label keeps the old strict rules.

sections.title: ROAs and Router Certificates
sections.content:
For a ROA whose end-entity certificate uses the new policy, each prefix in the ROA must be contained in the VRS-IP produced by validating that certificate. So a ROA is valid only if all its prefixes are encompassed by the VRS-IP of every certificate along the path to the trust anchor. Operators MAY issue a separate ROA for each prefix, so losing one prefix does not invalidate the others.

BGPsec Router Certificates (RFC 8209) get a similar rule: when they use the new policy, the VRS-AS MUST encompass all ASNs in the AS Identifier Delegation extension. Operators MAY issue separate certificates per ASN for the same reason.
sections.eli5: A stamp is only good if every place it names is still on the approved list. Making one stamp per place means one bad place cannot ruin the rest.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC walks through three trees. In each, CA1 holds 192.0.2.0/24, 2001:db8::/32 and AS64496, and CA2's certificate claims 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and AS64496, which overclaims 198.51.100.0/24.

  • Old OIDs only: CA2's certificate is invalid, so both ROAs and both BGPsec certificates below it are invalid.
  • New OIDs only: CA2's certificate is valid with a warning. The ROA for 192.0.2.0/24 is valid, the ROA for 198.51.100.0/24 is invalid, and a router certificate for AS64496 is valid. One covering AS64496-AS64497 is invalid because AS64497 is not in the VRS.
  • Mixed: new OIDs are used only on CA certificates where an overclaim is anticipated, such as CA2's, and old OIDs elsewhere. The outcomes match the new-only case.
sections.eli5: In the examples, one wrong line on one form no longer wrecks the neighbors. Only the item that really was not allowed gets rejected.

sections.title: Deployment and Security
sections.content:
The document defines the algorithm but does not dictate how it is deployed. Relying Party tools that do not yet implement the alternative profile will reject certificates using the new OIDs, so such tools need to be updated before CAs start using it. Because the OIDs are carried in each certificate, CAs need not migrate all at once, or even for all certificates.

On security, the authors believe the revised algorithm introduces no new vulnerabilities, because it cannot lead to a ROA or router certificate being accepted if it contains resources the issuer does not hold.
sections.eli5: Everyone who checks the tickets must learn the new rule first, or they will turn away tickets carrying the new label. But people can switch over one at a time.
